say: Noise-cancelling headphones make a roaring plane engine almost vanish. They don't block it. They fight sound with more sound.
Sound is a pressure wave. Air gets squeezed, then stretched, over and over, really fast, and your eardrum wiggles along.
First, a tiny mic on the outside of the ear cup listens to the noise around you, like a little spy.
Then a chip builds the exact opposite wave: every squeeze becomes a stretch, every peak a dip. Engineers call it anti-noise.
The speaker plays that anti-noise along with your music. Peak meets dip, they cancel out, and the drone just fades away.
Many headphones hide a second mic inside the cup. It checks what noise sneaked through, and the chip corrects it on the fly.
It works best on low, steady hums like engines. Voices and clattering dishes are higher and jumpier, so they're way harder.
For those higher sounds, the squishy cushions do the job, physically sealing your ears. Teamwork: soft foam plus clever math.
The idea is old! A German physicist patented it in the nineteen thirties, and pilots wore these long before your commute did.
So that silence is really two sounds fighting each other. Follow Simply Weird for more weird stuff like this.
